summary: On 17 July 2020 engineers responding to backbone congestion near Atlanta made a one-line router change that leaked all BGP routes into the backbone with a higher preference. Traffic across Cloudflare's network fell by about 50 percent for 27 minutes.

overview.background: Cloudflare's backbone links its data centers. Routers use BGP local-preference to choose paths, and local compute nodes had a preference of 100.
systems: Backbone links EWR to ORD and ATL to IAD
Data centers across North America, Europe, South America and Russia
overview.impact: Traffic across the network dropped about 50 percent. About 19 locations were affected, listed in the post, from 21:12 to 21:39 UTC. Logs and metrics were partly dropped from 21:47 to 22:10.
overview.severity: Global in effect, 27 minutes. Cloudflare says it was a configuration error, not an attack.
overview.gaps: The post does not give customer counts.

diagrams.title: Atlanta attracts the backbone's traffic
diagrams.caption: A change meant to withdraw routes leaked all BGP routes with local-preference 200. Other locations sent traffic to Atlanta, which could not handle it.

diagrams.title: Prefix limits and safer preference (conceptual)
diagrams.caption: Cloudflare planned a maximum-prefix limit on backbone BGP sessions and a change to local-preference so one location cannot attract others' traffic. This picture shows the idea.

timelineNote: Times are as published by the source. Entries without a clock time are given in order only.

timeline.e: The backbone link EWR to ORD is lost and ATL to IAD becomes congested.
Engineers make a change on the Atlanta router to remove some traffic.
Atlanta attracts traffic from across the backbone. The outage window starts.
Atlanta is dropped from the backbone. Traffic is restored.
Service is restored. Congestion at a core data center drops some logs until 22:10.
Full recovery, including logs and metrics.
A maximum-prefix limit on backbone BGP sessions is scheduled for deployment.

rootCause.trigger: A one-line change on the Atlanta router leaked all BGP routes into the backbone.
rootCause.underlying: The routes carried local-preference 200 against 100 for local compute nodes, so other locations preferred Atlanta for traffic that was not Atlanta's.
contributing: The correct change was to deactivate the term, not the prefix list
No maximum-prefix limit on backbone sessions
Local preference allowed one location to attract others' traffic

evidence.label: The change
evidence.body: a one line change started leaking all BGP routes into the backbone

evidence.label: The correct change
evidence.body: The correct change would have been to deactivate the term instead of the prefix-list.

evidence.label: A simulated prefix limit
evidence.body:
neighbor backbone-peer maximum-prefix 5000 warning-only 80
neighbor backbone-peer maximum-prefix 5000 teardown
evidence.note: Generic syntax showing a prefix limit that tears down a session if exceeded. Invented, not a vendor's exact syntax.

diagnose.step: Look at traffic by location and where it flows.
diagnose.why: Atlanta attracted traffic from across the backbone.

diagnose.step: Compare route preferences for local and backbone routes.

correct.step: Remove the affected location from the backbone and disable the router.
Apply a global change to prevent recurrence.

verify.step: Watch traffic return in each location.
Check logs and metrics catch up.
verify.why: They were lost for a short time.

prevent.step: Set maximum-prefix limits on backbone sessions.
Make local routes win over remote ones.
Use commit-confirm and peer review on router changes.

fix.safety: Removing a location from the backbone reduces capacity. Do it only when the location is the problem and traffic can be served elsewhere.

troubleshoot.scenario: Traffic halves and one router is overloaded. A change was made to it ten minutes ago to relieve congestion.
clues: Other sites send traffic to it
troubleshoot.question: How do you contain it?
hints: How do you take the router out?
troubleshoot.answer: Remove the router from the backbone, revert the term, confirm traffic recovers, then add prefix limits and change local preference.

options: Deactivate the term, not the prefix-list

remediation.answer: Set a limit above normal route counts and tear down above it.
Local routes get higher preference than routes learned from the backbone.
Require a second person and commit-confirm for router edits.

design.prompt: Design a backbone that survives a leaked route.
design.answer: Use prefix limits, route filters, local-first preference, staged changes and automatic rollback.

checks.q: How long was the outage window?

checks.why: Cloudflare says it was not an attack.
